Suezmax catching the VLCC fever

1⃣The hugely inefficient STS activities as a workaround to the Strait of Hormuz closure and increased Atlantic Basin arb crudes into the Far East have brought VLCC rates to a meteoric high, with TD3c printing WS1200, equivalent to $35/bbl for the journey from Ras Tanura to Ningbo. 

2⃣The Suezmax market has caught onto the craziness, with TD20 as a bellwether for this vessel class rising from WS250 at the start of September to now WS878. 

3⃣The dirty freight market is likely to heat up Aframaxes next, which will then also pull up LR2 rates in the clean side as more vessels look to dirty up their tonnage.

SG 10 E/W has been subject to extreme movements, much like the HOGO that was affected by the proposed US diesel export ban. 

1⃣The sudden weakness was due to the rise in ICE GO from an almost unimaginable tightness in Europe if US truly did ban exports and with Saudi cancelling cargoes into Europe due to the E/W pipeline outage. SG 10 E/W needed to make the Asian arbs work into Europe. 

2⃣The sudden increase was when China unceremoniously announced a suspension to product export quotas in October, followed by news of the G7 release of 100 mb of SPR barrels (crude and diesel), most of which is expected to be frontloaded by diesel and a commitment from US to avoid a ban. 

3⃣Sparta base case is for China to allow some diesel exports again after the Golden Week which should weaken SG 10 E/W back to the sub-100$/t levels.

Physical crude prices soar as oil futures stall

Physical crude prices have surged to the highest since the opening weeks of the war with Iran despite claims that increased tanker transits through the Strait of Hormuz and bypass pipelines have largely restored exports from the Gulf. 

Spot prices for the North Sea Forties crude stream (one of the largest components of the Brent crude complex) are currently being quoted over $140 per barrel, the highest since the war began. 

Forties output has been threatened after offshore workers voted to strike but prices had been climbing long before the industrial dispute came to a head.  

Dated Brent for immediate delivery has averaged more than $123 so far in October, passing the previous high of $116 in April, and the highest for more than four years, after adjusting for inflation. 

Cash prices for the principal crude grades from West Africa, among the main alternatives to Brent, are all quoted above $135. 

Physical prices are trading well above the front-month Brent futures contract, which has averaged just $102 so far in October. 

The gap between physical and futures prices is the widest since the war began and the broadest in records back for more than a decade ...

Politicians will always be politicians. Instead of realizing that the Strait of Hormuz issue + incoming global oil shortage won’t be resolved even after the SPR release, they are opting to buy time. Time the world doesn’t have, no matter how sizable the SPR is.
It’s like throwing bottles of water at a burning house. It’s not really going to do anything unless you solve the underlying issue.

The dilemma the world faces today is that the hefty inventory surplus has now turned into a deficit. China, which held a large crude oil surplus, is now buying crude. The world no longer benefits from the 4 to 5 million b/d reduction in Chinese crude imports. What was once seen as a headwind for the crude oil market is now turning into a tailwind. And despite many analysts pointing to higher Strait of Hormuz oil flows, the return of Chinese crude buying is the same black-box fundamental variable as the lack of buying.

If China buys the crude, which caused the Strait of Hormuz flow to increase, it has no relevance to the rest of the world. China is its own variable, black-box-in, black-box-out.

#Commodities
Softs: #Sugar futures jumped 4% on Monday to a 2024 high of 20.7 cents per pound, extending their recent strong run. While the latest move was underpinned by a 5% rally in the Brazilian real, an intensifying El Niño is adding to supply concerns, with excessive rainfall threatening production in Brazil while drought risks are rising in India and Thailand. These developments could potentially turn an expected sugar surplus into a deficit already this season. #Cocoa futures rose 3.5% on Monday, extending their weekly gain to 8%, as heavy rains in West Africa slowed sales, with flooded roads disrupting transport and wet conditions affecting bean quality.
Oil: #Brent traded lower on Monday, before bouncing ahead of USD 100 in Asia, as Gulf producers moved larger volumes through the Strait of Hormuz, with additional supply flowing through Saudi Arabia’s reopened East-West pipeline. Yet prices remain above USD 100 as a sizeable geopolitical risk premium persists amid the continued threat of renewed flare-ups. Iran, meanwhile, remains effectively blocked in, with dozens of laden tankers stranded along its coastline.
#Gold trades near key support just above USD 4,100, with macroeconomic headwinds from rising real yields and dollar strength continuing to weigh on investor appetite and fuel further long liquidation from hedge funds. With limited US economic data due this week, market focus will likely remain on the dollar, yields and ongoing political and fiscal turmoil in the Eurozone. A break below support just above USD 4,100 could signal a deeper retracement, while initial resistance is seen around USD 4,230.
